Source: https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/job-schedulers/repeat-strategies

# Repeat Strategies

BullMQ comes with two predefined strategies for creating repeatable jobs. The ‘every’ strategy is straightforward, allowing you to schedule jobs to repeat at specific intervals, measured in seconds. The more complex ‘cron’ strategy uses cron expressions, as defined by the [cron-parser](https://www.npmjs.com/package/cron-parser) to schedule jobs in intricate patterns. Additionally, BullMQ lets you create custom strategies, giving you the flexibility to define your own logic for setting job intervals.

### "Every" strategy

The every strategy is used when we simply want to produce repeatable jobs at specific intervals:

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const { Queue, Worker } = require('bullmq');

const connection = {
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 6379,
};

const myQueue = new Queue('my-repeatable-jobs', { connection });

// Upserting a repeatable job in the queue
await myQueue.upsertJobScheduler(
  'repeat-every-10s',
  {
    every: 10000, // Job will repeat every 10000 milliseconds (10 seconds)
  },
  {
    name: 'every-job',
    data: { jobData: 'data' },
    opts: {}, // Optional additional job options
  },
);

// Worker to process the jobs
const worker = new Worker(
  'my-repeatable-jobs',
  async job => {
    console.log(`Processing job ${job.id} with data: ${job.data.jobData}`);
  },
  { connection },
);
```

**Python**

```python
from bullmq import Queue, Worker

connection = {
    "host": "localhost",
    "port": 6379,
}

my_queue = Queue("my-repeatable-jobs", {"connection": connection})

# Upserting a repeatable job in the queue
await my_queue.upsertJobScheduler(
    "repeat-every-10s",
    {
        "every": 10000,  # Job will repeat every 10000 milliseconds (10 seconds)
    },
    job_name="every-job",
    job_data={"jobData": "data"},
    opts={},  # Optional additional job options
)

# Worker to process the jobs
async def process(job, token):
    print(f"Processing job {job.id} with data: {job.data['jobData']}")

worker = Worker("my-repeatable-jobs", process, {"connection": connection})
```

**Elixir**

```elixir
{:ok, _} = BullMQ.RedisConnection.start_link(name: :my_redis, host: "localhost", port: 6379)

# Upserting a repeatable job in the queue
{:ok, _job} =
  BullMQ.JobScheduler.upsert(
    :my_redis,
    "my-repeatable-jobs",
    "repeat-every-10s",
    # Job will repeat every 10000 milliseconds (10 seconds)
    %{every: 10000},
    "every-job",
    %{jobData: "data"},
    # Optional additional job options
    []
  )

# Worker to process the jobs
{:ok, worker} =
  BullMQ.Worker.start_link(
    queue: "my-repeatable-jobs",
    connection: :my_redis,
    processor: fn job ->
      IO.puts("Processing job #{job.id} with data: #{job.data["jobData"]}")
      :ok
    end
  )
```

**.NET**

```csharp
using System.Text.Json;
using BullMQ;

var connection = ConnectionOptions.FromString("localhost:6379");

var myQueue = new Queue("my-repeatable-jobs", new QueueOptions { Connection = connection });

// Upserting a repeatable job in the queue
await myQueue.UpsertJobSchedulerAsync(
    "repeat-every-10s",
    new RepeatOptions
    {
        Every = 10000, // Job will repeat every 10000 milliseconds (10 seconds)
    },
    new JobSchedulerTemplate
    {
        Name = "every-job",
        Data = new { jobData = "data" },
        Opts = new JobsOptions(), // Optional additional job options
    });

// Worker to process the jobs
var worker = new Worker(
    "my-repeatable-jobs",
    (job, _) =>
    {
        var data = (JsonElement)job.Data!;
        Console.WriteLine($"Processing job {job.Id} with data: {data.GetProperty("jobData")}");
        return Task.FromResult<object?>(null);
    },
    new WorkerOptions { Connection = connection });
```

**Rust**

```rust
use bullmq::job_scheduler::RepeatOptions;
use bullmq::options::RedisConnectionOptions;
use bullmq::worker::CancellationToken;
use bullmq::{Job, JobOptions, Queue, QueueOptions, Worker, WorkerOptions};

let connection = RedisConnectionOptions {
    host: Some("localhost".into()),
    port: Some(6379),
    ..Default::default()
};

let my_queue = Queue::with_options(
    "my-repeatable-jobs",
    QueueOptions::new().connection(connection.clone()),
)
.await?;

// Upserting a repeatable job in the queue
my_queue
    .upsert_job_scheduler(
        "repeat-every-10s",
        RepeatOptions {
            every: Some(10000), // Job will repeat every 10000 milliseconds (10 seconds)
            ..Default::default()
        },
        Some("every-job"),
        Some(serde_json::json!({ "jobData": "data" })),
        Some(JobOptions::new()), // Optional additional job options
    )
    .await?;

// Worker to process the jobs
let worker = Worker::with_options(
    "my-repeatable-jobs",
    |job: Job, _token: CancellationToken| async move {
        println!("Processing job {} with data: {}", job.id(), job.data()["jobData"]);
        Ok(serde_json::Value::Null)
    },
    WorkerOptions::new().connection(connection),
)
.await?;
```

### "Cron" strategy

The “cron” strategy in BullMQ leverages the [cron-parser](https://www.npmjs.com/package/cron-parser) library to use cron expressions for scheduling jobs with greater specificity. This approach is ideal for jobs requiring execution at precise times or intervals, such as automated reports or maintenance tasks.

Below is the supported format for cron expressions in cron-parser:

```
*    *    *    *    *    *
┬    ┬    ┬    ┬    ┬    ┬
│    │    │    │    │    │
│    │    │    │    │    └ day of week (0 - 7, 1L - 7L, where 0 or 7 is Sunday)
│    │    │    │    └───── month (1 - 12)
│    │    │    └────────── day of month (1 - 31, L for the last day of the month)
│    │    └─────────────── hour (0 - 23)
│    └──────────────────── minute (0 - 59)
└───────────────────────── second (0 - 59, optional)
```

This format includes the optional second field, which is not typically available in standard cron schedules, allowing for even more precise scheduling.

Cron expressions are quite powerful as in they support seamless handling timezone differences and daylight saving time transitions, crucial for tasks that depend on local times. And also because of the use of special characters to denote specific days or things like the last day of the month, providing flexibility for monthly and weekly tasks.

If you are new to Cron expressions, [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cron) is an excellent starting point to learn how to use them.

Here follows an example that sets up a job to execute at 9:00 AM from Monday to Friday:

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const { Queue, Worker } = require('bullmq');

const connection = {
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 6379,
};

const myQueue = new Queue('my-cron-jobs', { connection });

// Upserting a job with a cron expression
await myQueue.upsertJobScheduler(
  'weekday-morning-job',
  {
    pattern: '0 0 9 * * 1-5', // Runs at 9:00 AM every Monday to Friday
  },
  {
    name: 'cron-job',
    data: { jobData: 'morning data' },
    opts: {}, // Optional additional job options
  },
);

// Worker to process the jobs
const worker = new Worker(
  'my-cron-jobs',
  async job => {
    console.log(
      `Processing job ${job.id} at ${new Date()} with data: ${
        job.data.jobData
      }`,
    );
  },
  { connection },
);
```

**Python**

```python
from datetime import datetime
from bullmq import Queue, Worker

connection = {
    "host": "localhost",
    "port": 6379,
}

my_queue = Queue("my-cron-jobs", {"connection": connection})

# Upserting a job with a cron expression
await my_queue.upsertJobScheduler(
    "weekday-morning-job",
    {
        "pattern": "0 0 9 * * 1-5",  # Runs at 9:00 AM every Monday to Friday
    },
    job_name="cron-job",
    job_data={"jobData": "morning data"},
    opts={},  # Optional additional job options
)

# Worker to process the jobs
async def process(job, token):
    print(f"Processing job {job.id} at {datetime.now()} with data: {job.data['jobData']}")

worker = Worker("my-cron-jobs", process, {"connection": connection})
```

**Elixir**

```elixir
{:ok, _} = BullMQ.RedisConnection.start_link(name: :my_redis, host: "localhost", port: 6379)

# Upserting a job with a cron expression
# (the Elixir SDK uses standard 5-field cron expressions, without seconds)
{:ok, _job} =
  BullMQ.JobScheduler.upsert(
    :my_redis,
    "my-cron-jobs",
    "weekday-morning-job",
    # Runs at 9:00 AM every Monday to Friday
    %{pattern: "0 9 * * 1-5"},
    "cron-job",
    %{jobData: "morning data"},
    # Optional additional job options
    []
  )

# Worker to process the jobs
{:ok, worker} =
  BullMQ.Worker.start_link(
    queue: "my-cron-jobs",
    connection: :my_redis,
    processor: fn job ->
      IO.puts("Processing job #{job.id} at #{DateTime.utc_now()} with data: #{job.data["jobData"]}")
      :ok
    end
  )
```

**.NET**

```csharp
using System.Text.Json;
using BullMQ;

var connection = ConnectionOptions.FromString("localhost:6379");

var myQueue = new Queue("my-cron-jobs", new QueueOptions { Connection = connection });

// Upserting a job with a cron expression
await myQueue.UpsertJobSchedulerAsync(
    "weekday-morning-job",
    new RepeatOptions
    {
        Pattern = "0 0 9 * * 1-5", // Runs at 9:00 AM every Monday to Friday
    },
    new JobSchedulerTemplate
    {
        Name = "cron-job",
        Data = new { jobData = "morning data" },
        Opts = new JobsOptions(), // Optional additional job options
    });

// Worker to process the jobs
var worker = new Worker(
    "my-cron-jobs",
    (job, _) =>
    {
        var data = (JsonElement)job.Data!;
        Console.WriteLine(
            $"Processing job {job.Id} at {DateTime.Now} with data: {data.GetProperty("jobData")}");
        return Task.FromResult<object?>(null);
    },
    new WorkerOptions { Connection = connection });
```

**Rust**

```rust
use bullmq::job_scheduler::RepeatOptions;
use bullmq::options::RedisConnectionOptions;
use bullmq::worker::CancellationToken;
use bullmq::{Job, JobOptions, Queue, QueueOptions, Worker, WorkerOptions};

let connection = RedisConnectionOptions {
    host: Some("localhost".into()),
    port: Some(6379),
    ..Default::default()
};

let my_queue =
    Queue::with_options("my-cron-jobs", QueueOptions::new().connection(connection.clone())).await?;

// Upserting a job with a cron expression
my_queue
    .upsert_job_scheduler(
        "weekday-morning-job",
        RepeatOptions {
            pattern: Some("0 0 9 * * 1-5".into()), // Runs at 9:00 AM every Monday to Friday
            ..Default::default()
        },
        Some("cron-job"),
        Some(serde_json::json!({ "jobData": "morning data" })),
        Some(JobOptions::new()), // Optional additional job options
    )
    .await?;

// Worker to process the jobs
let worker = Worker::with_options(
    "my-cron-jobs",
    |job: Job, _token: CancellationToken| async move {
        println!(
            "Processing job {} at {:?} with data: {}",
            job.id(),
            std::time::SystemTime::now(),
            job.data()["jobData"]
        );
        Ok(serde_json::Value::Null)
    },
    WorkerOptions::new().connection(connection),
)
.await?;
```

### Custom Strategy

It is possible to define a different strategy to schedule repeatable jobs. The idea is that the repeat strategy, based on a pattern and the latest job's milliseconds, return the next desired timestamp. Although not used in the following example, you could have different behaviours on your repeat strategies based on the current job's name if you want to. However note that **only** **one** repeatStrategy can be defined for a given queue.

The strategy receives the scheduler's repeat options, which also include a read-only `count` with the number of iterations already produced. It is managed internally and is only defined when the worker picks up a job to schedule the next iteration, before that job's processor runs; it cannot be set through `upsertJobScheduler`.

For example we can create a custom one for [RRULE](https://jkbrzt.github.io/rrule/) like this:

```typescript
import { JobSchedulerRepeatOptions, Queue, Worker } from 'bullmq';
import { rrulestr } from 'rrule';

const settings = {
  repeatStrategy: (
    millis: number,
    opts: JobSchedulerRepeatOptions,
    _jobName: string,
  ) => {
    const currentDate =
      opts.startDate && new Date(opts.startDate) > new Date(millis)
        ? new Date(opts.startDate)
        : new Date(millis);

    const rrule = rrulestr(opts.pattern);

    if (rrule.origOptions.count && !rrule.origOptions.dtstart) {
      throw new Error('DTSTART must be defined to use COUNT with rrule');
    }

    const next_occurrence = rrule.after(currentDate, false);
    return next_occurrence?.getTime();
  },
};

const myQueue = new Queue('Paint', { settings });

// Repeat job every 10 seconds
await myQueue.upsertJobScheduler(
  'collibris',
  {
    pattern: 'RRULE:FREQ=SECONDLY;INTERVAL=10;WKST=MO',
  },
  {
    data: { color: 'green' },
  },
);

// Repeat job every 20 seconds
await myQueue.upsertJobScheduler(
  'pingeons',
  {
    pattern: 'RRULE:FREQ=SECONDLY;INTERVAL=20;WKST=MO',
  },
  {
    data: { color: 'gray' },
  },
);

const worker = new Worker(
  'Paint',
  async () => {
    doSomething();
  },
  { settings },
);
```

> **Danger:** As you may have noticed, the repeat strategy setting should be provided in **both** the Queue and Worker classes. The reason we need it in both places is that when we first add the job to the Queue, we need to calculate when the next iteration will occur. After that, the Worker takes over, and we use the settings configured in the Worker.

---

Source: https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/job-schedulers/repeat-options

# Repeat options

There are some options that can be used on all Job Schedulers, to control some aspects of the repetitions. Lets review them one by one:

#### Start date

This option sets a future date from which the job will start being scheduled. This can be useful for setting up jobs that should begin repeating on a specific day.

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const { Queue } = require('bullmq');
const connection = { host: 'localhost', port: 6379 };
const myQueue = new Queue('my-dated-jobs', { connection });

await myQueue.upsertJobScheduler(
  'start-later-job',
  {
    every: 60000, // every minute
    startDate: new Date('2024-10-15T00:00:00Z'), // start on October 15, 2024
  },
  {
    name: 'timed-start-job',
    data: { message: 'Starting later' },
  },
);
```

**Python**

```python
from bullmq import Queue

connection = {"host": "localhost", "port": 6379}
my_queue = Queue("my-dated-jobs", {"connection": connection})

await my_queue.upsertJobScheduler(
    "start-later-job",
    {
        "every": 60000,  # every minute
        "startDate": "2024-10-15T00:00:00Z",  # start on October 15, 2024
    },
    job_name="timed-start-job",
    job_data={"message": "Starting later"},
)
```

**Elixir**

```elixir
{:ok, _} = BullMQ.RedisConnection.start_link(name: :my_redis, host: "localhost", port: 6379)

{:ok, _job} =
  BullMQ.JobScheduler.upsert(
    :my_redis,
    "my-dated-jobs",
    "start-later-job",
    %{
      # every minute
      every: 60000,
      # start on October 15, 2024
      start_date: ~U[2024-10-15 00:00:00Z]
    },
    "timed-start-job",
    %{message: "Starting later"}
  )
```

**.NET**

```csharp
using BullMQ;

var connection = ConnectionOptions.FromString("localhost:6379");
var myQueue = new Queue("my-dated-jobs", new QueueOptions { Connection = connection });

await myQueue.UpsertJobSchedulerAsync(
    "start-later-job",
    new RepeatOptions
    {
        Every = 60000, // every minute
        StartDate = "2024-10-15T00:00:00Z", // start on October 15, 2024
    },
    new JobSchedulerTemplate
    {
        Name = "timed-start-job",
        Data = new { message = "Starting later" },
    });
```

**Rust**

```rust
use bullmq::job_scheduler::RepeatOptions;
use bullmq::options::RedisConnectionOptions;
use bullmq::{Queue, QueueOptions};

let connection = RedisConnectionOptions {
    host: Some("localhost".into()),
    port: Some(6379),
    ..Default::default()
};
let my_queue =
    Queue::with_options("my-dated-jobs", QueueOptions::new().connection(connection)).await?;

my_queue
    .upsert_job_scheduler(
        "start-later-job",
        RepeatOptions {
            every: Some(60000),                // every minute
            start_date: Some(1728950400000), // start on October 15, 2024 (Unix ms)
            ..Default::default()
        },
        Some("timed-start-job"),
        Some(serde_json::json!({ "message": "Starting later" })),
        None,
    )
    .await?;
```

#### End Date

Use this to specify when the job should stop being scheduled, effectively setting an expiration date for the job repetitions.

**TypeScript**

```typescript
await myQueue.upsertJobScheduler(
  'end-soon-job',
  {
    every: 60000, // every minute
    endDate: new Date('2024-11-01T00:00:00Z'), // end on November 1, 2024
  },
  {
    name: 'timed-end-job',
    data: { message: 'Ending soon' },
  },
);
```

**Python**

```python
await my_queue.upsertJobScheduler(
    "end-soon-job",
    {
        "every": 60000,  # every minute
        "endDate": "2024-11-01T00:00:00Z",  # end on November 1, 2024
    },
    job_name="timed-end-job",
    job_data={"message": "Ending soon"},
)
```

**Elixir**

```elixir
{:ok, _job} =
  BullMQ.JobScheduler.upsert(
    :my_redis,
    "my-dated-jobs",
    "end-soon-job",
    %{
      # every minute
      every: 60000,
      # end on November 1, 2024
      end_date: ~U[2024-11-01 00:00:00Z]
    },
    "timed-end-job",
    %{message: "Ending soon"}
  )
```

**.NET**

```csharp
await myQueue.UpsertJobSchedulerAsync(
    "end-soon-job",
    new RepeatOptions
    {
        Every = 60000, // every minute
        EndDate = "2024-11-01T00:00:00Z", // end on November 1, 2024
    },
    new JobSchedulerTemplate
    {
        Name = "timed-end-job",
        Data = new { message = "Ending soon" },
    });
```

**Rust**

```rust
my_queue
    .upsert_job_scheduler(
        "end-soon-job",
        RepeatOptions {
            every: Some(60000),              // every minute
            end_date: Some(1730419200000), // end on November 1, 2024 (Unix ms)
            ..Default::default()
        },
        Some("timed-end-job"),
        Some(serde_json::json!({ "message": "Ending soon" })),
        None,
    )
    .await?;
```

#### Timezone (`tz`)

Use `tz` to evaluate cron patterns in a specific timezone.

**TypeScript**

```typescript
await myQueue.upsertJobScheduler(
  'utc-cron-job',
  {
    pattern: '0 15 3 * * *',
    tz: 'UTC',
  },
  {
    name: 'utc-execution-job',
    data: { message: 'Runs at 03:15 UTC' },
  },
);
```

**Python**

```python
await my_queue.upsertJobScheduler(
    "utc-cron-job",
    {
        "pattern": "0 15 3 * * *",
        "tz": "UTC",
    },
    job_name="utc-execution-job",
    job_data={"message": "Runs at 03:15 UTC"},
)
```

**.NET**

```csharp
await myQueue.UpsertJobSchedulerAsync(
    "utc-cron-job",
    new RepeatOptions
    {
        Pattern = "0 15 3 * * *",
        Tz = "UTC",
    },
    new JobSchedulerTemplate
    {
        Name = "utc-execution-job",
        Data = new { message = "Runs at 03:15 UTC" },
    });
```

**Rust**

```rust
my_queue
    .upsert_job_scheduler(
        "utc-cron-job",
        RepeatOptions {
            pattern: Some("0 15 3 * * *".into()),
            tz: Some("UTC".into()),
            ..Default::default()
        },
        Some("utc-execution-job"),
        Some(serde_json::json!({ "message": "Runs at 03:15 UTC" })),
        None,
    )
    .await?;
```

> **Note:** If you previously used `repeat.utc`, replace it with `tz: 'UTC'`.

#### Limit

This setting is used to limit the number of times a job will be repeated. When the count reaches this limit, no more jobs will be produced for the given job scheduler.

**TypeScript**

```typescript
await myQueue.upsertJobScheduler(
  'limited-job',
  {
    every: 10000, // every 10 seconds
    limit: 10, // limit to 10 executions
  },
  {
    name: 'limited-execution-job',
    data: { message: 'Limited runs' },
  },
);
```

**Python**

```python
await my_queue.upsertJobScheduler(
    "limited-job",
    {
        "every": 10000,  # every 10 seconds
        "limit": 10,  # limit to 10 executions
    },
    job_name="limited-execution-job",
    job_data={"message": "Limited runs"},
)
```

**Elixir**

```elixir
{:ok, _job} =
  BullMQ.JobScheduler.upsert(
    :my_redis,
    "my-dated-jobs",
    "limited-job",
    %{
      # every 10 seconds
      every: 10000,
      # limit to 10 executions
      limit: 10
    },
    "limited-execution-job",
    %{message: "Limited runs"}
  )
```

**.NET**

```csharp
await myQueue.UpsertJobSchedulerAsync(
    "limited-job",
    new RepeatOptions
    {
        Every = 10000, // every 10 seconds
        Limit = 10, // limit to 10 executions
    },
    new JobSchedulerTemplate
    {
        Name = "limited-execution-job",
        Data = new { message = "Limited runs" },
    });
```

**Rust**

```rust
my_queue
    .upsert_job_scheduler(
        "limited-job",
        RepeatOptions {
            every: Some(10000), // every 10 seconds
            limit: Some(10),    // limit to 10 executions
            ..Default::default()
        },
        Some("limited-execution-job"),
        Some(serde_json::json!({ "message": "Limited runs" })),
        None,
    )
    .await?;
```

#### immediately

This setting forces the job to execute as soon as it is added, regardless of the schedule. This can help in situations where an immediate action is required before entering a regular cycle.

When you use the every option in BullMQ, it schedules jobs based on fixed time intervals, which might seem a bit counterintuitive initially. For instance, if you set an interval of 2000ms, jobs will be triggered at every even second—such as 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 seconds, and so on. This means the scheduling aligns with the clock, regardless of when you actually added the job.

If you need a job to begin processing immediately after you add a job scheduler, regardless of the interval’s alignment with the clock, you can use the immediately setting. This is especially crucial for long intervals. For example, if you set the job to repeat monthly, normally it would wait to start until the first second of the next month. If you add the job mid-month, it would not start until the beginning of the following month. Using immediately ensures the first instance of the job runs as soon as it’s added, bypassing the wait until the scheduled interval begins.

**TypeScript**

```typescript
await myQueue.upsertJobScheduler(
  'immediate-job',
  {
    every: 86400000, // once a day
    immediately: true, // execute the first one immediately
  },
  {
    name: 'instant-job',
    data: { message: 'Immediate start' },
  },
);
```

**Python**

```python
await my_queue.upsertJobScheduler(
    "immediate-job",
    {
        "every": 86400000,  # once a day
        "immediately": True,  # execute the first one immediately
    },
    job_name="instant-job",
    job_data={"message": "Immediate start"},
)
```

**Elixir**

```elixir
{:ok, _job} =
  BullMQ.JobScheduler.upsert(
    :my_redis,
    "my-dated-jobs",
    "immediate-job",
    %{
      # once a day
      every: 86400000,
      # execute the first one immediately
      immediately: true
    },
    "instant-job",
    %{message: "Immediate start"}
  )
```

**.NET**

```csharp
await myQueue.UpsertJobSchedulerAsync(
    "immediate-job",
    new RepeatOptions
    {
        Every = 86400000, // once a day
        Immediately = true, // execute the first one immediately
    },
    new JobSchedulerTemplate
    {
        Name = "instant-job",
        Data = new { message = "Immediate start" },
    });
```

**Rust**

```rust
my_queue
    .upsert_job_scheduler(
        "immediate-job",
        RepeatOptions {
            every: Some(86400000),   // once a day
            immediately: Some(true), // execute the first one immediately
            ..Default::default()
        },
        Some("instant-job"),
        Some(serde_json::json!({ "message": "Immediate start" })),
        None,
    )
    .await?;
```

> **Danger:** From version 5.19.0 and onwards the "immediately" option has been deprecated. The current behaviour is as if "immediately" was always true, in other words, the first repetition will always be immediately for a new inserted job scheduler, and then repeat according to the "every" setting. Subsequent calls to upsertJobScheduler for **existing** schedulers will not lead to immediate repetitions and will instead follow the "every" interval.

---

Source: https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/job-schedulers/manage-job-schedulers

# Manage Job Schedulers

In BullMQ, managing the lifecycle and inventory of job schedulers is crucial for maintaining efficient and organized background tasks. In addition to the upsertJobScheduler method—which allows for the addition and updating of job schedulers—two other methods play essential roles: removeJobScheduler and getJobSchedulers. These functions enable the removal of schedulers and retrieval of all existing schedulers, respectively, providing comprehensive control over your job scheduling environment.

The scheduler ID passed to `upsertJobScheduler` is returned as the `key` property by `getJobScheduler` and `getJobSchedulers`. Use this `key` when retrieving, updating, or removing a scheduler. It is distinct from the scheduler's `name` and the IDs of the jobs it produces; the optional `id` property on `JobSchedulerJson` is not the scheduler identifier.

#### Remove job scheduler

The **removeJobScheduler** method is designed to delete a specific job scheduler from the queue. This is particularly useful when a scheduled task is no longer needed or if you wish to clean up inactive or obsolete schedulers to optimize resource usage.

**TypeScript**

```typescript
// Remove a job scheduler with ID 'scheduler-123'
const result = await queue.removeJobScheduler('scheduler-123');
console.log(
  result ? 'Scheduler removed successfully' : 'Missing Job Scheduler',
);
```

**Python**

```python
# Remove a job scheduler with ID 'scheduler-123'
# (the Python SDK returns 0 when the scheduler was removed, 1 when it was missing)
result = await queue.removeJobScheduler("scheduler-123")
print(
    "Scheduler removed successfully" if result == 0 else "Missing Job Scheduler"
)
```

**Elixir**

```elixir
# Remove a job scheduler with ID 'scheduler-123'
{:ok, result} = BullMQ.JobScheduler.remove(:my_redis, "my-queue", "scheduler-123")

IO.puts(if(result, do: "Scheduler removed successfully", else: "Missing Job Scheduler"))
```

**.NET**

```csharp
// Remove a job scheduler with ID 'scheduler-123'
var result = await queue.RemoveJobSchedulerAsync("scheduler-123");
Console.WriteLine(
    result ? "Scheduler removed successfully" : "Missing Job Scheduler");
```

**Rust**

```rust
// Remove a job scheduler with ID 'scheduler-123'
let result = queue.remove_job_scheduler("scheduler-123").await?;
println!(
    "{}",
    if result { "Scheduler removed successfully" } else { "Missing Job Scheduler" }
);
```

The method will return true if there was a Job Scheduler to remove with the given ID, or false if there wasn't any.

#### Get Job Schedulers

The **getJobSchedulers** method retrieves a list of all configured job schedulers within a specified range. This is invaluable for monitoring and managing multiple job schedulers, especially in systems where jobs are dynamically scheduled and require frequent reviews or adjustments.

**TypeScript**

```typescript
// Retrieve the first 10 job schedulers in ascending order of their next execution time
const schedulers = await queue.getJobSchedulers(0, 9, true);
console.log('Current job schedulers:', schedulers);
```

**Python**

```python
# Retrieve the first 10 job schedulers in ascending order of their next execution time
schedulers = await queue.getJobSchedulers(0, 9, True)
print("Current job schedulers:", schedulers)
```

**Elixir**

```elixir
# Retrieve the first 10 job schedulers in ascending order of their next execution time
{:ok, schedulers} =
  BullMQ.JobScheduler.list(:my_redis, "my-queue", start: 0, end: 9, asc: true)

IO.inspect(schedulers, label: "Current job schedulers")
```

**.NET**

```csharp
// Retrieve the first 10 job schedulers in ascending order of their next execution time
var schedulers = await queue.GetJobSchedulersAsync(0, 9, true);
Console.WriteLine($"Current job schedulers: {JsonSerializer.Serialize(schedulers)}");
```

**Rust**

```rust
// Retrieve the first 10 job schedulers in ascending order of their next execution time
let schedulers = queue.get_job_schedulers(0, 9, true).await?;
println!("Current job schedulers: {:?}", schedulers);
```

For example, to remove a scheduler returned by `getJobSchedulers`, pass its `key` to `removeJobScheduler`:

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const [scheduler] = await queue.getJobSchedulers(0, 0);
if (scheduler) {
  await queue.removeJobScheduler(scheduler.key);
}
```

**Python**

```python
schedulers = await queue.getJobSchedulers(0, 0)
if schedulers:
    await queue.removeJobScheduler(schedulers[0]["key"])
```

**Elixir**

```elixir
case BullMQ.JobScheduler.list(:my_redis, "my-queue", start: 0, end: 0) do
  {:ok, [scheduler | _]} ->
    BullMQ.JobScheduler.remove(:my_redis, "my-queue", scheduler.key)

  _ ->
    :ok
end
```

**.NET**

```csharp
var schedulers = await queue.GetJobSchedulersAsync(0, 0);
if (schedulers.Count > 0)
{
    await queue.RemoveJobSchedulerAsync(schedulers[0].Key);
}
```

**Rust**

```rust
let schedulers = queue.get_job_schedulers(0, 0, false).await?;
if let Some(scheduler) = schedulers.first() {
    queue.remove_job_scheduler(&scheduler.key).await?;
}
```

This method can be particularly useful for generating reports or dashboards that provide insights into when jobs are scheduled to run, aiding in system monitoring and troubleshooting.

#### Get Job Scheduler

The **getJobScheduler** method retrieves a job scheduler by id. This is invaluable for inspecting dedicated configurations.

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const scheduler = await queue.getJobScheduler('test');
console.log('Current job scheduler:', scheduler);
```

**Python**

```python
scheduler = await queue.getJobScheduler("test")
print("Current job scheduler:", scheduler)
```

**Elixir**

```elixir
{:ok, scheduler} = BullMQ.JobScheduler.get(:my_redis, "my-queue", "test")
IO.inspect(scheduler, label: "Current job scheduler")
```

**.NET**

```csharp
var scheduler = await queue.GetJobSchedulerAsync("test");
Console.WriteLine($"Current job scheduler: {JsonSerializer.Serialize(scheduler)}");
```

**Rust**

```rust
let scheduler = queue.get_job_scheduler("test").await?;
println!("Current job scheduler: {:?}", scheduler);
```

## Read more:

- 💡 [Remove Job Scheduler API Reference](https://docs.bullmq.io/api/classes/v6.Queue.html#removejobscheduler)
- 💡 [Get Job Schedulers API Reference](https://docs.bullmq.io/api/classes/v6.Queue.html#getjobschedulers)
- 💡 [Get Job Scheduler API Reference](https://docs.bullmq.io/api/classes/v6.Queue.html#getjobscheduler)

Source: https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/flows/

# Flows

BullMQ supports parent - child relationships between jobs. The basic idea is that a parent job will not be moved to the wait status (i.e. where it could be picked up by a worker) until all its children jobs have been processed successfully. Apart from that, a parent or a child job are no different from regular jobs.

This functionality enables the creation of flows where jobs are the node of trees of arbitrary depth.

> **Warning:** Flows are added to a queue using the `FlowProducer` class.

In order to create "flows" you must use the [`FlowProducer`](https://docs.bullmq.io/api/classes/v6.FlowProducer.html) class. The [_**`add`**_](https://docs.bullmq.io/api/classes/v6.FlowProducer.html#add) method accepts an object with the following interface:

```typescript
interface FlowJobBase<T> {
  name: string;
  queueName: string;
  data?: any;
  prefix?: string;
  opts?: Omit<T, 'debounce' | 'deduplication' | 'repeat'>;
  children?: FlowChildJob[];
}

type FlowChildJob = FlowJobBase<
  Omit<JobsOptions, 'debounce' | 'deduplication' | 'parent' | 'repeat'>
>;

type FlowJob = FlowJobBase<JobsOptions>;
```

So we can add a flow like this one:

**TypeScript**

```typescript
import { FlowProducer } from 'bullmq';

// A FlowProducer constructor takes an optional "connection"
// object otherwise it connects to a local redis instance.
const flowProducer = new FlowProducer();

const flow = await flowProducer.add({
  name: 'renovate-interior',
  queueName: 'renovate',
  children: [
    { name: 'paint', data: { place: 'ceiling' }, queueName: 'steps' },
    { name: 'paint', data: { place: 'walls' }, queueName: 'steps' },
    { name: 'fix', data: { place: 'floor' }, queueName: 'steps' },
  ],
});
```

**Python**

```python
from bullmq import FlowProducer

# A FlowProducer constructor takes an optional "connection"
# object otherwise it connects to a local redis instance.
flowProducer = FlowProducer()

flow = await flowProducer.add({
    "name": "renovate-interior",
    "queueName": "renovate",
    "children": [
        {"name": "paint", "data": {"place": "ceiling"}, "queueName": "steps"},
        {"name": "paint", "data": {"place": "walls"}, "queueName": "steps"},
        {"name": "fix", "data": {"place": "floor"}, "queueName": "steps"},
    ],
})
```

**Elixir**

```elixir
# The Elixir FlowProducer requires a "connection" option
# pointing to a started Redis connection.
{:ok, flow} =
  BullMQ.FlowProducer.add(
    %{
      name: "renovate-interior",
      queue_name: "renovate",
      children: [
        %{name: "paint", data: %{place: "ceiling"}, queue_name: "steps"},
        %{name: "paint", data: %{place: "walls"}, queue_name: "steps"},
        %{name: "fix", data: %{place: "floor"}, queue_name: "steps"}
      ]
    },
    connection: :my_redis
  )
```

**.NET**

```csharp
using BullMQ;

// A FlowProducer constructor takes a "Connection" option
// pointing to your Redis instance.
var flowProducer = new FlowProducer(new QueueBaseOptions
{
    Connection = ConnectionOptions.FromString("localhost:6379"),
});

var flow = await flowProducer.AddAsync(new FlowJob
{
    Name = "renovate-interior",
    QueueName = "renovate",
    Children = new[]
    {
        new FlowJob { Name = "paint", Data = new { place = "ceiling" }, QueueName = "steps" },
        new FlowJob { Name = "paint", Data = new { place = "walls" }, QueueName = "steps" },
        new FlowJob { Name = "fix", Data = new { place = "floor" }, QueueName = "steps" },
    },
});
```

**Rust**

```rust
use bullmq::{FlowJob, FlowProducer};
use serde_json::json;

// FlowProducer::new() connects to a local Redis instance,
// use FlowProducer::with_options to pass a custom connection.
let flow_producer = FlowProducer::new().await?;

let flow = flow_producer
    .add(
        FlowJob::new("renovate-interior", "renovate", json!({}))?
            .add_child(FlowJob::new("paint", "steps", json!({ "place": "ceiling" }))?)
            .add_child(FlowJob::new("paint", "steps", json!({ "place": "walls" }))?)
            .add_child(FlowJob::new("fix", "steps", json!({ "place": "floor" }))?),
    )
    .await?;
```

The above code will atomically add 4 jobs: one to the "renovate" queue, and 3 to the "steps" queue. When the 3 jobs in the "steps" queue are completed, the parent job in the "renovate" queue will be processed as a regular job.

The above call will return instances for all the jobs added to the queue.

> **Note:** Note that the parent queue does not need to be the same queue as the one used for the children.

> **Warning:** If a jobId option is provided, make sure that it does not contain a colon **:** as this is considered a separator.

> **Warning:** Do not use deduplication options on flow nodes. When a child is deduplicated against an existing job, it may not be attached to its parent, so the parent can become eligible before that requested child work completes. A future breaking release will reject deduplication on every flow node; each child addition must have a known job ID so its dependency can be attached reliably.

When the parent job is processed it is possible to access the results generated by its child jobs. For example, lets assume the following worker for the child jobs:

**TypeScript**

```typescript
import { Worker } from 'bullmq';

const stepsWorker = new Worker('steps', async job => {
  await performStep(job.data);

  if (job.name === 'paint') {
    return 2500;
  } else if (job.name === 'fix') {
    return 1750;
  }
});
```

**Python**

```python
from bullmq import Worker

async def process(job, token):
    await performStep(job.data)

    if job.name == "paint":
        return 2500
    elif job.name == "fix":
        return 1750

stepsWorker = Worker("steps", process)
```

**Elixir**

```elixir
{:ok, steps_worker} =
  BullMQ.Worker.start_link(
    queue: "steps",
    connection: :my_redis,
    processor: fn job ->
      perform_step(job.data)

      case job.name do
        "paint" -> {:ok, 2500}
        "fix" -> {:ok, 1750}
        _ -> :ok
      end
    end
  )
```

**.NET**

```csharp
using BullMQ;

var stepsWorker = new Worker(
    "steps",
    async (job, _) =>
    {
        await PerformStep(job.Data);

        return job.Name switch
        {
            "paint" => 2500,
            "fix" => 1750,
            _ => null,
        };
    },
    new WorkerOptions { Connection = ConnectionOptions.FromString("localhost:6379") });
```

**Rust**

```rust
use bullmq::worker::CancellationToken;
use bullmq::{Job, Worker};

let steps_worker = Worker::new("steps", |job: Job, _token: CancellationToken| async move {
    perform_step(job.data()).await;

    match job.name() {
        "paint" => Ok(serde_json::json!(2500)),
        "fix" => Ok(serde_json::json!(1750)),
        _ => Ok(serde_json::Value::Null),
    }
})
.await?;
```

We can implement a parent worker that sums the costs of the children's jobs using the `getChildrenValues` method. This method returns an object with _job keys_ as keys and the _result of that given job_ as a value:

**TypeScript**

```typescript
import { Worker } from 'bullmq';

const renovateWorker = new Worker('renovate', async job => {
  const childrenValues = await job.getChildrenValues();

  const totalCosts = Object.values(childrenValues).reduce(
    (prev, cur) => prev + cur,
    0,
  );

  await sendInvoice(totalCosts);
});
```

**Python**

```python
from bullmq import Worker

async def process(job, token):
    childrenValues = await job.getChildrenValues()

    totalCosts = sum(childrenValues.values())

    await sendInvoice(totalCosts)

renovateWorker = Worker("renovate", process)
```

**Elixir**

```elixir
{:ok, renovate_worker} =
  BullMQ.Worker.start_link(
    queue: "renovate",
    connection: :my_redis,
    processor: fn job ->
      {:ok, children_values} = BullMQ.Job.get_children_values(job)

      total_costs = children_values |> Map.values() |> Enum.sum()

      send_invoice(total_costs)
      :ok
    end
  )
```

**.NET**

```csharp
using System.Text.Json;
using BullMQ;

var renovateWorker = new Worker(
    "renovate",
    async (job, _) =>
    {
        var childrenValues = await job.GetChildrenValuesAsync();

        var totalCosts = childrenValues.Values.Sum(value => ((JsonElement)value!).GetDouble());

        await SendInvoice(totalCosts);
        return null;
    },
    new WorkerOptions { Connection = ConnectionOptions.FromString("localhost:6379") });
```

**Rust**

```rust
use bullmq::worker::CancellationToken;
use bullmq::{Job, Worker};

let renovate_worker = Worker::new("renovate", |job: Job, _token: CancellationToken| async move {
    let children_values = job.get_children_values().await?;

    let total_costs: f64 = children_values.values().filter_map(|value| value.as_f64()).sum();

    send_invoice(total_costs).await;
    Ok(serde_json::Value::Null)
})
.await?;
```

It is possible to add as deep job hierarchies as needed. See the following example where jobs are depending on each other, allowing serial execution of jobs:

**TypeScript**

```typescript
import { FlowProducer } from 'bullmq';
const flowProducer = new FlowProducer();

const queueName = 'assembly-line';
const chain = await flowProducer.add({
  name: 'car',
  data: { step: 'engine' },
  queueName,
  children: [
    {
      name: 'car',
      data: { step: 'wheels' },
      queueName,
      children: [{ name: 'car', data: { step: 'chassis' }, queueName }],
    },
  ],
});
```

**Python**

```python
from bullmq import FlowProducer

flowProducer = FlowProducer()

queueName = "assembly-line"
chain = await flowProducer.add({
    "name": "car",
    "data": {"step": "engine"},
    "queueName": queueName,
    "children": [
        {
            "name": "car",
            "data": {"step": "wheels"},
            "queueName": queueName,
            "children": [{"name": "car", "data": {"step": "chassis"}, "queueName": queueName}],
        },
    ],
})
```

**Elixir**

```elixir
queue_name = "assembly-line"

{:ok, chain} =
  BullMQ.FlowProducer.add(
    %{
      name: "car",
      data: %{step: "engine"},
      queue_name: queue_name,
      children: [
        %{
          name: "car",
          data: %{step: "wheels"},
          queue_name: queue_name,
          children: [%{name: "car", data: %{step: "chassis"}, queue_name: queue_name}]
        }
      ]
    },
    connection: :my_redis
  )
```

**.NET**

```csharp
using BullMQ;

var flowProducer = new FlowProducer(new QueueBaseOptions
{
    Connection = ConnectionOptions.FromString("localhost:6379"),
});

const string queueName = "assembly-line";
var chain = await flowProducer.AddAsync(new FlowJob
{
    Name = "car",
    Data = new { step = "engine" },
    QueueName = queueName,
    Children = new[]
    {
        new FlowJob
        {
            Name = "car",
            Data = new { step = "wheels" },
            QueueName = queueName,
            Children = new[]
            {
                new FlowJob { Name = "car", Data = new { step = "chassis" }, QueueName = queueName },
            },
        },
    },
});
```

**Rust**

```rust
use bullmq::{FlowJob, FlowProducer};
use serde_json::json;

let flow_producer = FlowProducer::new().await?;

let queue_name = "assembly-line";
let chain = flow_producer
    .add(
        FlowJob::new("car", queue_name, json!({ "step": "engine" }))?.add_child(
            FlowJob::new("car", queue_name, json!({ "step": "wheels" }))?
                .add_child(FlowJob::new("car", queue_name, json!({ "step": "chassis" }))?),
        ),
    )
    .await?;
```

In this case one job will be processed after the previous one has been completed.

> **Note:** The order of processing would be: `chassis`, `wheels` and finally `engine`.

## Getters

There are some special getters that can be used in order to get jobs related to a flow. First, we have a method in the `Job` class to get all the dependencies for a given job:

```typescript
const dependencies = await job.getDependencies();
```

it will return all the **direct** **dependencies** (i.e. the children of a given job).

Or if you want to get specific types of children:

```typescript
// cursors are used in pagination
const { processed, nextProcessedCursor } = await job.getDependencies({
  processed: {
    count: 5,
    cursor: 0,
  },
});

const { unprocessed, nextUnprocessedCursor } = await job.getDependencies({
  unprocessed: {
    count: 5,
    cursor: 0,
  },
});

const { failed, nextFailedCursor } = await job.getDependencies({
  failed: {
    count: 5,
    cursor: 0,
  },
});

const { ignored, nextIgnoredCursor } = await job.getDependencies({
  ignored: {
    count: 5,
    cursor: 0,
  },
});
```

The `Job` class also provides some other methods that we presented above

## Get Dependencies Count

To get all the different counts of children by type:

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const { failed, ignored, processed, unprocessed } =
  await job.getDependenciesCount();
```

**Rust**

```rust
let bullmq::DependenciesCount {
    failed,
    ignored,
    processed,
    unprocessed,
} = job.get_dependencies_count().await?;
```

Or if you want to be specific:

```typescript
const { failed } = await job.getDependenciesCount({
  failed: true,
});

const { ignored, processed } = await job.getDependenciesCount({
  ignored: true,
  processed: true,
});

const { unprocessed } = await job.getDependenciesCount({
  unprocessed: true,
});
```

## Get Children Values

To get all the values produced by the children of a given job:

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const values = await job.getChildrenValues();
```

**Python**

```python
values = await job.getChildrenValues()
```

**Elixir**

```elixir
{:ok, values} = BullMQ.Job.get_children_values(job)
```

**.NET**

```csharp
var values = await job.GetChildrenValuesAsync();
```

**Rust**

```rust
let values = job.get_children_values().await?;
```

Also, a new property is available in the `Job` class, _**`parentKey`,**_ with a fully qualified key for the job parent.

Finally, there is also a new state which a job can be in, "waiting-children", for parent jobs that have not yet had their children completed:

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const state = await job.getState();
// state will be "waiting-children"
```

**Python**

```python
state = await job.getState()
# state will be "waiting-children"
```

**Elixir**

```elixir
{:ok, state} = BullMQ.Queue.get_job_state(job.queue_name, job.id, connection: :my_redis)
# state will be :waiting_children
```

**.NET**

```csharp
var state = await job.GetStateAsync();
// state will be JobState.WaitingChildren
```

**Rust**

```rust
let state = job.get_state().await?;
// state will be JobState::WaitingChildren
```

## Provide options

When adding a flow it is also possible to provide an extra object **`queueOptions`** object, in which you can add your specific options for every queue that is used in the flow. These options would affect each one of the jobs that are added to the flow using the `FlowProducer`.

**TypeScript**

```typescript
import { FlowProducer } from 'bullmq';
const flowProducer = new FlowProducer();

const queueName = 'assembly-line';
const chain = await flowProducer.add(
  {
    name: 'car',
    data: { step: 'engine' },
    queueName,
    children: [
      {
        name: 'car',
        data: { step: 'wheels' },
        queueName,
      },
    ],
  },
  {
    queuesOptions: {
      [queueName]: {
        defaultJobOptions: {
          removeOnComplete: true,
        },
      },
    },
  },
);
```

**Python**

```python
from bullmq import FlowProducer

flowProducer = FlowProducer()

queueName = "assembly-line"
chain = await flowProducer.add(
    {
        "name": "car",
        "data": {"step": "engine"},
        "queueName": queueName,
        "children": [
            {
                "name": "car",
                "data": {"step": "wheels"},
                "queueName": queueName,
            },
        ],
    },
    {
        "queuesOptions": {
            queueName: {
                "defaultJobOptions": {
                    "removeOnComplete": True,
                },
            },
        },
    },
)
```

**Rust**

```rust
use bullmq::types::RemoveOnFinish;
use bullmq::{FlowJob, FlowOptions, FlowProducer, FlowQueueOptions, JobOptions};
use serde_json::json;

let flow_producer = FlowProducer::new().await?;

let queue_name = "assembly-line";
let chain = flow_producer
    .add_with_opts(
        FlowJob::new("car", queue_name, json!({ "step": "engine" }))?
            .add_child(FlowJob::new("car", queue_name, json!({ "step": "wheels" }))?),
        &FlowOptions::new().queue(
            queue_name,
            FlowQueueOptions::new()
                .default_job_options(JobOptions::new().remove_on_complete(RemoveOnFinish::Bool(true))),
        ),
    )
    .await?;
```

> **Warning:** Queue options are defined in the context of their instances. You should provide your configurations in the second parameter in order to avoid unexpected behaviors.

## Jobs removal

BullMQ also provides seamless removal functionality for jobs that are part of a flow.

When removing a job that is part of the flow there are several important considerations:

1. If a parent job is removed, all its children will also be removed.
2. If a child job is removed, its parent dependency to said child is also removed, and if the child was the last child in the dependencies list, the parent job will be completed.
3. Since a job can be both a parent and a child in a large flow, both 1 and 2 will occur if removing such a job.
4. If any of the jobs that would be removed happen to be locked, none of the jobs will be removed, and an exception will be thrown.

Apart from the considerations above, removing a job can simply be done by either using the `Job` or the `Queue` class:

**TypeScript**

```typescript
await job.remove();
// or
await queue.remove(job.id);
```

**Python**

```python
await job.remove()
# or
await queue.remove(job.id)
```

**Elixir**

```elixir
BullMQ.Queue.remove_job(job.queue_name, job.id, connection: :my_redis, remove_children: true)
```

**.NET**

```csharp
await job.RemoveAsync();
// or
await queue.RemoveAsync(job.Id!);
```

**Rust**

```rust
queue.remove(job.id()).await?;
```

**PHP**

```php
$queue->remove($job->id);
```

## Read more:

- 📋 [Divide large jobs using flows](https://blog.taskforce.sh/splitting-heavy-jobs-using-bullmq-flows/)
- 💡 [FlowProducer API Reference](https://docs.bullmq.io/api/classes/v6.FlowProducer.html)
- 💡 [Job API Reference](https://docs.bullmq.io/api/classes/v6.Job.html)
- 💡 [Get Children Values API Reference](https://docs.bullmq.io/api/classes/v6.Job.html#getchildrenvalues)
- 💡 [Get Dependencies API Reference](https://docs.bullmq.io/api/classes/v6.Job.html#getdependencies)
- 💡 [Get Dependencies Count API Reference](https://docs.bullmq.io/api/classes/v6.Job.html#getdependenciescount)

Source: https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/flows/adding-bulks

# Adding flows in bulk

Sometimes it is necessary to atomically add flows in bulk. For example, there could be a requirement that all the flows must be created or none of them. Also, adding flows in bulk can be faster since it reduces the number of roundtrips to Redis:

**TypeScript**

```typescript
import { FlowProducer } from 'bullmq';

const flow = new FlowProducer({ connection });

const trees = await flow.addBulk([
  {
    name: 'root-job-1',
    queueName: 'rootQueueName-1',
    data: {},
    children: [
      {
        name,
        data: { idx: 0, foo: 'bar' },
        queueName: 'childrenQueueName-1',
      },
    ],
  },
  {
    name: 'root-job-2',
    queueName: 'rootQueueName-2',
    data: {},
    children: [
      {
        name,
        data: { idx: 1, foo: 'baz' },
        queueName: 'childrenQueueName-2',
      },
    ],
  },
]);
```

**Python**

```python
from bullmq import FlowProducer

flow = FlowProducer({"connection": connection})

trees = await flow.addBulk([
    {
        "name": "root-job-1",
        "queueName": "rootQueueName-1",
        "data": {},
        "children": [
            {
                "name": name,
                "data": {"idx": 0, "foo": "bar"},
                "queueName": "childrenQueueName-1",
            },
        ],
    },
    {
        "name": "root-job-2",
        "queueName": "rootQueueName-2",
        "data": {},
        "children": [
            {
                "name": name,
                "data": {"idx": 1, "foo": "baz"},
                "queueName": "childrenQueueName-2",
            },
        ],
    },
])
```

**Elixir**

```elixir
{:ok, trees} =
  BullMQ.FlowProducer.add_bulk(
    [
      %{
        name: "root-job-1",
        queue_name: "rootQueueName-1",
        data: %{},
        children: [
          %{
            name: name,
            data: %{idx: 0, foo: "bar"},
            queue_name: "childrenQueueName-1"
          }
        ]
      },
      %{
        name: "root-job-2",
        queue_name: "rootQueueName-2",
        data: %{},
        children: [
          %{
            name: name,
            data: %{idx: 1, foo: "baz"},
            queue_name: "childrenQueueName-2"
          }
        ]
      }
    ],
    connection: :my_redis
  )
```

**Rust**

```rust
use bullmq::{FlowJob, FlowProducer, FlowProducerOptions};
use serde_json::json;

let flow = FlowProducer::with_options(FlowProducerOptions::new().connection(connection)).await?;

let trees = flow
    .add_bulk(vec![
        FlowJob::new("root-job-1", "rootQueueName-1", json!({}))?.add_child(FlowJob::new(
            name,
            "childrenQueueName-1",
            json!({ "idx": 0, "foo": "bar" }),
        )?),
        FlowJob::new("root-job-2", "rootQueueName-2", json!({}))?.add_child(FlowJob::new(
            name,
            "childrenQueueName-2",
            json!({ "idx": 1, "foo": "baz" }),
        )?),
    ])
    .await?;
```

This call can only succeed or fail, and all or none of the jobs will be added.

- 💡 [Add Bulk API Reference](https://docs.bullmq.io/api/classes/v6.FlowProducer.html#addbulk)

# Get Flow Tree

In some situations, you need to get a job and all of its children, grandchildren, and so on.

The pattern to solve this requirement consists of using the [`getFlow`](https://docs.bullmq.io/api/classes/v6.FlowProducer.html#getflow) method.

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const flow = new FlowProducer({ connection });

const originalTree = await flow.add({
  name: 'root-job',
  queueName: 'topQueueName',
  data: {},
  children: [
    {
      name,
      data: { idx: 0, foo: 'bar' },
      queueName: 'childrenQueueName',
      children: [
        {
          name,
          data: { idx: 4, foo: 'baz' },
          queueName: 'grandchildrenQueueName',
        },
      ],
    },
    {
      name,
      data: { idx: 2, foo: 'foo' },
      queueName: 'childrenQueueName',
    },
    {
      name,
      data: { idx: 3, foo: 'bis' },
      queueName: 'childrenQueueName',
    },
  ],
});

const { job: topJob } = originalTree;

const tree = await flow.getFlow({
  id: topJob.id,
  queueName: 'topQueueName',
});

const { children, job } = tree;
```

**Rust**

```rust
use bullmq::{FlowJob, FlowProducer, FlowProducerOptions, GetFlowOptions, JobNode};
use serde_json::json;

let flow = FlowProducer::with_options(FlowProducerOptions::new().connection(connection)).await?;

let original_tree = flow
    .add(
        FlowJob::new("root-job", "topQueueName", json!({}))?
            .add_child(
                FlowJob::new(name, "childrenQueueName", json!({ "idx": 0, "foo": "bar" }))?
                    .add_child(FlowJob::new(
                        name,
                        "grandchildrenQueueName",
                        json!({ "idx": 4, "foo": "baz" }),
                    )?),
            )
            .add_child(FlowJob::new(name, "childrenQueueName", json!({ "idx": 2, "foo": "foo" }))?)
            .add_child(FlowJob::new(name, "childrenQueueName", json!({ "idx": 3, "foo": "bis" }))?),
    )
    .await?;

let top_job = &original_tree.job;

let tree = flow
    .get_flow(GetFlowOptions::new("topQueueName", top_job.id()))
    .await?;

let JobNode { children, job } = tree;
```

> **Note:** Each _child_ may have a `job` property and in the case they have children as well, they would have the `children` property

You may also need a way to limit that information if you have many children for one of the job nodes.

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const limitedTree = await flow.getFlow({
  id: topJob.id,
  queueName: 'topQueueName',
  depth: 1, // get only the first level of children
  maxChildren: 2, // get only 2 children per node
});

const { children, job } = limitedTree;
```

**Rust**

```rust
let limited_tree = flow
    .get_flow(
        GetFlowOptions::new("topQueueName", top_job.id())
            .depth(1) // get only the first level of children
            .max_children(2), // get only 2 children per node
    )
    .await?;

let JobNode { children, job } = limited_tree;
```

## Read more:

- 💡 [Get Flow API Reference](https://docs.bullmq.io/api/classes/v6.FlowProducer.html#getflow)

Source: https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/flows/fail-parent

# Fail Parent

In certain workflows, you may need a parent job to fail immediately if any of its child jobs fail. The `failParentOnFailure` option allows you to achieve this behaviour. When set to true on a child job, it ensures that if the child fails, its parent job is also marked as failed. This effect can propagate recursively up the job hierarchy, potentially causing grandparents or higher-level ancestors to fail as well, depending on the configuration.

### Key Points

- Selective Application: Only child jobs with failParentOnFailure: true will trigger the failure of their parent job upon failing. Child jobs without this option will not affect the parent's state if they fail.
- Recursive Behavior: If a child with this option fails, and its parent also has failParentOnFailure: true, the failure propagates upward through the job tree, potentially affecting grandparents and beyond.
- Immediate Effect: As soon as a qualifying child job fails, the parent job is moved to the failed state.

### Example

**TypeScript**

```typescript
import { FlowProducer } from 'bullmq';

const flow = new FlowProducer({ connection });

const originalTree = await flow.add({
  name: 'root-job',
  queueName: 'topQueueName',
  data: {},
  children: [
    {
      name: 'child-job',
      data: { idx: 0, foo: 'bar' },
      queueName: 'childrenQueueName',
      // This child will fail its parent if it fails
      opts: { failParentOnFailure: true },
      children: [
        {
          name,
          data: { idx: 1, foo: 'bah' },
          queueName: 'grandChildrenQueueName',
          // This grandchild will fail its parent if it fails
          opts: { failParentOnFailure: true },
        },
        {
          name,
          data: { idx: 2, foo: 'baz' },
          queueName: 'grandChildrenQueueName',
          // No failParentOnFailure; its failure won't affect the parent
        },
      ],
    },
    {
      name,
      data: { idx: 3, foo: 'foo' },
      queueName: 'childrenQueueName',
      // No failParentOnFailure; its failure won't affect the parent
    },
  ],
});
```

**Python**

```python
from bullmq import FlowProducer

flow = FlowProducer({"connection": connection})

originalTree = await flow.add({
    "name": "root-job",
    "queueName": "topQueueName",
    "data": {},
    "children": [
        {
            "name": "child-job",
            "data": {"idx": 0, "foo": "bar"},
            "queueName": "childrenQueueName",
            # This child will fail its parent if it fails
            "opts": {"failParentOnFailure": True},
            "children": [
                {
                    "name": name,
                    "data": {"idx": 1, "foo": "bah"},
                    "queueName": "grandChildrenQueueName",
                    # This grandchild will fail its parent if it fails
                    "opts": {"failParentOnFailure": True},
                },
                {
                    "name": name,
                    "data": {"idx": 2, "foo": "baz"},
                    "queueName": "grandChildrenQueueName",
                    # No failParentOnFailure; its failure won't affect the parent
                },
            ],
        },
        {
            "name": name,
            "data": {"idx": 3, "foo": "foo"},
            "queueName": "childrenQueueName",
            # No failParentOnFailure; its failure won't affect the parent
        },
    ],
})
```

**Elixir**

```elixir
{:ok, original_tree} =
  BullMQ.FlowProducer.add(
    %{
      name: "root-job",
      queue_name: "topQueueName",
      data: %{},
      children: [
        %{
          name: "child-job",
          data: %{idx: 0, foo: "bar"},
          queue_name: "childrenQueueName",
          # This child will fail its parent if it fails
          opts: %{fail_parent_on_failure: true},
          children: [
            %{
              name: name,
              data: %{idx: 1, foo: "bah"},
              queue_name: "grandChildrenQueueName",
              # This grandchild will fail its parent if it fails
              opts: %{fail_parent_on_failure: true}
            },
            %{
              name: name,
              data: %{idx: 2, foo: "baz"},
              queue_name: "grandChildrenQueueName"
              # No fail_parent_on_failure; its failure won't affect the parent
            }
          ]
        },
        %{
          name: name,
          data: %{idx: 3, foo: "foo"},
          queue_name: "childrenQueueName"
          # No fail_parent_on_failure; its failure won't affect the parent
        }
      ]
    },
    connection: :my_redis
  )
```

**Rust**

```rust
use bullmq::{FlowJob, FlowProducer, FlowProducerOptions, JobOptions};
use serde_json::json;

let flow = FlowProducer::with_options(FlowProducerOptions::new().connection(connection)).await?;

let original_tree = flow
    .add(
        FlowJob::new("root-job", "topQueueName", json!({}))?
            .add_child(
                FlowJob::new("child-job", "childrenQueueName", json!({ "idx": 0, "foo": "bar" }))?
                    // This child will fail its parent if it fails
                    .options(JobOptions::new().fail_parent_on_failure())
                    .add_child(
                        FlowJob::new(name, "grandChildrenQueueName", json!({ "idx": 1, "foo": "bah" }))?
                            // This grandchild will fail its parent if it fails
                            .options(JobOptions::new().fail_parent_on_failure()),
                    )
                    // No fail_parent_on_failure; its failure won't affect the parent
                    .add_child(FlowJob::new(
                        name,
                        "grandChildrenQueueName",
                        json!({ "idx": 2, "foo": "baz" }),
                    )?),
            )
            // No fail_parent_on_failure; its failure won't affect the parent
            .add_child(FlowJob::new(name, "childrenQueueName", json!({ "idx": 3, "foo": "foo" }))?),
    )
    .await?;
```

> **Note:** As soon as a _child_ with this option fails, the parent job will be marked as failed lazily. A worker must process the parent job before it transitions to the failed state. The failure will result in an _UnrecoverableError_ with the message **child {childKey} failed**. Additionally, this option will be validated recursively, meaning a grandparent or higher-level ancestor could also fail depending on the configuration.

### How it Works

- If grandchild-job-1 fails, its parent (child-job-1) will fail because of failParentOnFailure: true. Since child-job-1 also has failParentOnFailure: true, the root job (root-job) will fail as well.
- If grandchild-job-2 fails, its parent (child-job-1) will not fail because failParentOnFailure is not set on this grandchild.
- Similarly, if child-job-2 fails, the root job will remain unaffected since failParentOnFailure is not enabled for that child.

### Use Case

This option is particularly useful in workflows where the success of a parent job depends critically on specific child jobs, allowing you to enforce strict dependencies and fail fast when necessary.

## Read more:

- 💡 [Add Flow API Reference](https://docs.bullmq.io/api/classes/v6.FlowProducer.html#add)

---

Source: https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/flows/continue-parent

# Continue Parent

> **Note:** Available since v5.58.0

The `continueParentOnFailure` option allows a parent job to start processing as soon as a child job fails, while the `removeUnprocessedChildren` method enables dynamic cleanup of unprocessed child jobs. Additionally, you can use the `getFailedChildrenValues`() method to determine whether the parent is processing due to a child failure or because all children completed successfully, allowing you to define distinct logic paths.

### continueParentOnFailure

When set to `true` on a child job, the `continueParentOnFailure` option causes the parent job to begin processing immediately if that child fails. This contrasts with the default behavior, where the parent waits for all children to finish.

- **Key Behavior**: The parent moves to the active state as soon as a child with this option fails, even if other children are still running or unprocessed.
- **Use Case**: Ideal for scenarios where a child’s failure requires immediate parent intervention, such as aborting the workflow or performing cleanup.

### removeUnprocessedChildren

This method, available on a job instance, removes all unprocessed child jobs (those in waiting or delayed states) from the queue. It’s particularly useful when paired with `continueParentOnFailure` to get rid of remaining children after a failure.

- **Key Behavior**: Only affects children that haven’t started processing; **active, completed or failed** children remain intact.
- **Usage**: Call within the parent’s processor to clean up dynamically.

### getFailedChildrenValues

The `getFailedChildrenValues()` method returns an object mapping the IDs of failed child jobs to their failure error messages. This allows the parent job to determine why it’s processing—whether due to a child failure (triggered by `continueParentOnFailure`) or because all children completed successfully.

- **Return Value**: An object where keys are job IDs and values are error messages (e.g., { "job-id-1": "Upload failed" }). If no children failed, the object is empty.
- **Usage**: Use this in the parent’s processor to branch logic based on the presence of failed children.

### Example

The following example shows how to combine these features, with the parent job reacting differently based on whether a child failed or all children succeeded:

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const { FlowProducer } = require('bullmq');
const flow = new FlowProducer({ connection });

// Define the flow
const originalTree = await flow.add({
  name: 'root-job',
  queueName: 'topQueueName',
  data: {},
  children: [
    {
      name: 'child-job-1',
      data: { idx: 0, foo: 'bar' },
      queueName: 'childrenQueueName',
      opts: { continueParentOnFailure: true }, // Parent processes if this child fails
    },
    {
      name: 'child-job-2',
      data: { idx: 1, foo: 'baz' },
      queueName: 'childrenQueueName',
    },
    {
      name: 'child-job-3',
      data: { idx: 2, foo: 'qux' },
      queueName: 'childrenQueueName',
    },
  ],
});

// Processor for the parent job
const processor = async job => {
  // Check if any children failed
  const failedChildren = await job.getFailedChildrenValues();
  const hasFailedChildren = Object.keys(failedChildren).length > 0;

  if (hasFailedChildren) {
    // Path 1: A child failed, triggering continueParentOnFailure
    console.log(
      `Parent job ${job.name} triggered by child failure(s):`,
      failedChildren,
    );

    // Remove unprocessed children
    await job.removeUnprocessedChildren();
    console.log('Unprocessed child jobs have been removed.');

    // Additional cleanup or error handling can go here
  } else {
    // Path 2: All children completed successfully
    console.log(
      `Parent job ${job.name} processing after all children completed successfully.`,
    );

    // Proceed with normal parent logic (e.g., aggregating results)
  }
};
```

**Rust**

```rust
use bullmq::worker::CancellationToken;
use bullmq::{FlowJob, FlowProducer, FlowProducerOptions, Job, JobOptions, Queue, QueueOptions};
use serde_json::json;

let flow = FlowProducer::with_options(FlowProducerOptions::new().connection(connection.clone())).await?;

// Define the flow
let original_tree = flow
    .add(
        FlowJob::new("root-job", "topQueueName", json!({}))?
            .add_child(
                FlowJob::new("child-job-1", "childrenQueueName", json!({ "idx": 0, "foo": "bar" }))?
                    .options(JobOptions::new().continue_parent_on_failure()), // Parent processes if this child fails
            )
            .add_child(FlowJob::new("child-job-2", "childrenQueueName", json!({ "idx": 1, "foo": "baz" }))?)
            .add_child(FlowJob::new("child-job-3", "childrenQueueName", json!({ "idx": 2, "foo": "qux" }))?),
    )
    .await?;

// Used to remove the unprocessed children of the parent job
let top_queue = Queue::with_options("topQueueName", QueueOptions::new().connection(connection)).await?;

// Processor for the parent job
let processor = move |job: Job, _token: CancellationToken| {
    let top_queue = top_queue.clone();
    async move {
        // Check if any children failed
        let failed_children = job.get_failed_children_values().await?;
        let has_failed_children = !failed_children.is_empty();

        if has_failed_children {
            // Path 1: A child failed, triggering continue_parent_on_failure
            println!(
                "Parent job {} triggered by child failure(s): {:?}",
                job.name(),
                failed_children
            );

            // Remove unprocessed children
            top_queue.remove_unprocessed_children(job.id()).await?;
            println!("Unprocessed child jobs have been removed.");

            // Additional cleanup or error handling can go here
        } else {
            // Path 2: All children completed successfully
            println!(
                "Parent job {} processing after all children completed successfully.",
                job.name()
            );

            // Proceed with normal parent logic (e.g., aggregating results)
        }

        Ok::<_, bullmq::Error>(serde_json::Value::Null)
    }
};
```

### Practical use case

Consider a workflow where child jobs upload files to different servers. If one upload fails (e.g., `child-job-1`), the parent can use continueParentOnFailure to react immediately, check `getFailedChildrenValues()` to confirm the failure, and call `removeUnprocessedChildren()` to cancel remaining uploads. If all uploads succeed, the parent might aggregate the results instead.

---

Source: https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/flows/remove-dependency

# Remove Dependency

In some situations, you may have a parent job and need to remove the relationship when one of its children fail.

The pattern to solve this requirement consists on using the **removeDependencyOnFailure** option. This option will make sure that when a job fails, the dependency is removed from the parent, so the parent will complete without waiting for the failed children.

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const flow = new FlowProducer({ connection });

const originalTree = await flow.add({
  name: 'root-job',
  queueName: 'topQueueName',
  data: {},
  children: [
    {
      name,
      data: { idx: 0, foo: 'bar' },
      queueName: 'childrenQueueName',
      opts: { removeDependencyOnFailure: true },
      children: [
        {
          name,
          data: { idx: 1, foo: 'bah' },
          queueName: 'grandChildrenQueueName',
        },
        {
          name,
          data: { idx: 2, foo: 'baz' },
          queueName: 'grandChildrenQueueName',
        },
      ],
    },
    {
      name,
      data: { idx: 3, foo: 'foo' },
      queueName: 'childrenQueueName',
    },
  ],
});
```

**Python**

```python
flow = FlowProducer({"connection": connection})

originalTree = await flow.add({
    "name": "root-job",
    "queueName": "topQueueName",
    "data": {},
    "children": [
        {
            "name": name,
            "data": {"idx": 0, "foo": "bar"},
            "queueName": "childrenQueueName",
            "opts": {"removeDependencyOnFailure": True},
            "children": [
                {
                    "name": name,
                    "data": {"idx": 1, "foo": "bah"},
                    "queueName": "grandChildrenQueueName",
                },
                {
                    "name": name,
                    "data": {"idx": 2, "foo": "baz"},
                    "queueName": "grandChildrenQueueName",
                },
            ],
        },
        {
            "name": name,
            "data": {"idx": 3, "foo": "foo"},
            "queueName": "childrenQueueName",
        },
    ],
})
```

**Elixir**

```elixir
{:ok, original_tree} =
  BullMQ.FlowProducer.add(
    %{
      name: "root-job",
      queue_name: "topQueueName",
      data: %{},
      children: [
        %{
          name: name,
          data: %{idx: 0, foo: "bar"},
          queue_name: "childrenQueueName",
          opts: %{remove_dependency_on_failure: true},
          children: [
            %{
              name: name,
              data: %{idx: 1, foo: "bah"},
              queue_name: "grandChildrenQueueName"
            },
            %{
              name: name,
              data: %{idx: 2, foo: "baz"},
              queue_name: "grandChildrenQueueName"
            }
          ]
        },
        %{
          name: name,
          data: %{idx: 3, foo: "foo"},
          queue_name: "childrenQueueName"
        }
      ]
    },
    connection: :my_redis
  )
```

**Rust**

```rust
use bullmq::{FlowJob, FlowProducer, FlowProducerOptions, JobOptions};
use serde_json::json;

let flow = FlowProducer::with_options(FlowProducerOptions::new().connection(connection)).await?;

let original_tree = flow
    .add(
        FlowJob::new("root-job", "topQueueName", json!({}))?
            .add_child(
                FlowJob::new(name, "childrenQueueName", json!({ "idx": 0, "foo": "bar" }))?
                    .options(JobOptions::new().remove_dependency_on_failure())
                    .add_child(FlowJob::new(
                        name,
                        "grandChildrenQueueName",
                        json!({ "idx": 1, "foo": "bah" }),
                    )?)
                    .add_child(FlowJob::new(
                        name,
                        "grandChildrenQueueName",
                        json!({ "idx": 2, "foo": "baz" }),
                    )?),
            )
            .add_child(FlowJob::new(name, "childrenQueueName", json!({ "idx": 3, "foo": "foo" }))?),
    )
    .await?;
```

> **Note:** As soon as a **child** with this option fails, the parent job will be moved to a waiting state only if there are no more pending children.

- 💡 [Add Flow API Reference](https://docs.bullmq.io/api/classes/v6.FlowProducer.html#add)
